name: Deltoid
parts: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle
etymology: From Greek delta (the triangular letter Δ) + -eidēs ‘shaped like’ (via Latin deltoides). So it means ‘the triangle-shaped muscle’ — an inverted Δ capping the shoulder.
origin: Lateral third of clavicle (anterior border), lateral margin and superior surface of acromion, and inferior lip of the spine of the scapula
insertion: Deltoid tuberosity of humerus
actions: Shoulder abduction (acromial part, beyond the first ~15°)
Shoulder flexion and internal rotation (clavicular part)
Shoulder extension and external rotation (spinal part)
tip: Shoulder dislocations or surgical-neck fractures can injure the axillary nerve — check sensation over the “regimental badge” area and deltoid strength.

name: Anterior deltoid (clavicular part)
etymology: From Greek delta (the triangular letter Δ) + -eidēs ‘shaped like’ (via Latin deltoides). So it means ‘the triangle-shaped muscle’ — an inverted Δ capping the shoulder. ‘Clavicular’ is from Latin clavicula ‘little key’ — the part arising from the collarbone.
origin: Anterior border and superior surface of lateral third of clavicle
insertion: Deltoid tuberosity of humerus
tip: Heavily loaded by pressing (bench, overhead press) — usually needs less isolation work than the middle and posterior delts.

name: Middle deltoid (acromial part)
etymology: From Greek delta (the triangular letter Δ) + -eidēs ‘shaped like’ (via Latin deltoides). So it means ‘the triangle-shaped muscle’ — an inverted Δ capping the shoulder. ‘Acromial’ is from Greek akron ‘tip’ + ōmos ‘shoulder’ — the part arising from the acromion, the tip of the shoulder.
origin: Lateral margin and superior surface of acromion
insertion: Deltoid tuberosity of humerus
actions: Shoulder abduction (prime mover after the first ~15°)
Shoulder abduction in the scapular plane
tip: Multipennate, so it is strong but short-ranged; lateral raises train it, and supraspinatus helps initiate abduction.

name: Posterior deltoid (spinal part)
parts: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle
etymology: From Greek delta (the triangular letter Δ) + -eidēs ‘shaped like’ (via Latin deltoides). So it means ‘the triangle-shaped muscle’ — an inverted Δ capping the shoulder. ‘Spinal’ refers to the spine of the scapula (Latin spina ‘thorn’), from which this part arises.
origin: Inferior lip of the crest of the spine of the scapula
insertion: Deltoid tuberosity of humerus
tip: Often underdeveloped relative to the front delts — face pulls and reverse flyes help balance pressing-dominant programmes.

name: Pectoralis major
parts: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle
Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle
Abdominal part of pectoralis major muscle
etymology: From Latin pectoralis ‘of the chest’ (pectus, breast) + major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger chest muscle’ (vs pectoralis minor beneath it).
origin: Clavicular head: anterior surface of medial half of clavicle; sternocostal head: anterior surface of sternum and costal cartilages 1–6; abdominal part: aponeurosis of external oblique (anterior rectus sheath)
insertion: Lateral lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of humerus (crest of greater tubercle)
actions: Shoulder extension from a flexed position (sternocostal head)
innervation: Lateral pectoral nerve (C5–C7) and medial pectoral nerve (C8–T1)
tip: Its tendon twists so the lower fibres insert highest — ruptures usually happen at the bottom of a heavy bench press.

name: Pectoralis major — clavicular head
parts: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle
etymology: From Latin pectoralis ‘of the chest’ (pectus, breast) + major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger chest muscle’ (vs pectoralis minor beneath it). ‘Clavicular’ is from Latin clavicula ‘little key’ — the head arising from the collarbone.
origin: Anterior surface of medial half of clavicle
insertion: Lateral lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of humerus
tip: Emphasised by incline pressing and low-to-high cable flyes, because its fibres run upward toward the clavicle.

name: Pectoralis major — sternocostal head
parts: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle
etymology: From Latin pectoralis ‘of the chest’ (pectus, breast) + major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger chest muscle’ (vs pectoralis minor beneath it). ‘Sternocostal’ is from Greek sternon ‘chest, breastbone’ + Latin costa ‘rib’ — the head arising from the sternum and rib cartilages.
origin: Anterior surface of sternum and costal cartilages 1–6
insertion: Lateral lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of humerus
actions: Shoulder extension from a flexed position
tip: The bulk of the pec — flat and decline pressing, dips and high-to-low flyes load it most.

name: Pectoralis major — abdominal part
parts: Abdominal part of pectoralis major muscle
etymology: From Latin pectoralis ‘of the chest’ (pectus, breast) + major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger chest muscle’ (vs pectoralis minor beneath it). ‘Abdominal’ is from Latin abdomen ‘belly’ — the slip arising from the abdominal wall aponeurosis.
origin: Aponeurosis of external oblique muscle (anterior layer of rectus sheath)
insertion: Lateral lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of humerus (highest, deepest fibres of the twisted tendon)
actions: Shoulder extension from a flexed position
tip: Inconstant: a small slip from the rectus sheath that some people lack. Its fibres twist to insert highest on the humerus and are most stretched at the bottom of a wide bench press, the commonest site of pec tears.

name: Pectoralis minor
etymology: From Latin pectoralis ‘of the chest’ (pectus, breast) + minor ‘smaller’. So it means ‘the smaller chest muscle’, lying under pectoralis major.
origin: Anterior surfaces of ribs 3–5 near their costal cartilages
insertion: Medial border and superior surface of the coracoid process of scapula
actions: Elevates ribs 3–5 in forced inspiration (scapula fixed)
innervation: Medial pectoral nerve (C8–T1), with a contribution from the lateral pectoral nerve
tip: A short pec minor tilts the scapula forward (rounded shoulders) and can compress the brachial plexus beneath it (pectoralis minor / thoracic outlet syndrome).

name: Subclavius
etymology: From Latin sub ‘under’ + clavis/clavicula ‘(little) key, collarbone’. So it means ‘the muscle under the clavicle’.
origin: Junction of the 1st rib and its costal cartilage
insertion: Subclavian groove on the inferior surface of the middle third of the clavicle
tip: Cushions the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus if the clavicle is fractured.

name: Serratus anterior
etymology: From Latin serratus ‘saw-toothed’ (serra, saw) + anterior ‘in front’. So it means ‘the saw-toothed muscle at the front (side) of the chest’ — its rib slips look like saw teeth.
origin: External surfaces of the lateral parts of ribs 1–8 (often 1–9)
insertion: Anterior (costal) surface of the medial border of the scapula, from superior to inferior angle
actions: Holds the scapula against the thoracic wall
tip: Long thoracic nerve injury causes medial scapular winging; the “plus” phase of a push-up-plus trains it.

name: Supraspinatus
etymology: From Latin supra ‘above’ + spina ‘spine’. So it means ‘the muscle above the spine (of the scapula)’, filling the supraspinous fossa.
origin: Medial two-thirds of the supraspinous fossa of scapula
insertion: Superior facet of the greater tubercle of humerus
actions: Stabilises the humeral head in the glenoid (rotator cuff)
tip: Rotator cuff = SITS (Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis); supraspinatus is the most commonly impinged and torn — test with empty/full can.

name: Infraspinatus
etymology: From Latin infra ‘below’ + spina ‘spine’. So it means ‘the muscle below the spine (of the scapula)’, filling the infraspinous fossa.
origin: Medial two-thirds of the infraspinous fossa of scapula
insertion: Middle facet of the greater tubercle of humerus
actions: Stabilises the humeral head in the glenoid (rotator cuff)
tip: The main external rotator of the cuff — side-lying or cable external rotations target it; suprascapular nerve entrapment at the spinoglenoid notch weakens it alone.

name: Teres minor
etymology: From Latin teres ‘round, smooth (rounded off)’ + minor ‘smaller’. So it means ‘the smaller round muscle’ (vs teres major below it).
origin: Upper two-thirds of the posterior surface of the lateral border of scapula
insertion: Inferior facet of the greater tubercle of humerus
actions: Stabilises the humeral head in the glenoid (rotator cuff)
tip: A rotator cuff muscle (SITS) supplied by the axillary nerve, not the suprascapular; the hornblower’s sign tests it.

name: Subscapularis
etymology: From Latin sub ‘under’ + scapula ‘shoulder blade’. So it means ‘the muscle under (on the front of) the shoulder blade’, filling the subscapular fossa.
origin: Subscapular fossa (anterior surface of scapula)
insertion: Lesser tubercle of humerus (and anterior shoulder capsule)
actions: Stabilises the humeral head anteriorly (rotator cuff)
tip: The only rotator cuff muscle on the lesser tubercle (the “S” facing forward in SITS); test with the lift-off or belly-press test.

name: Teres major
etymology: From Latin teres ‘round, smooth (rounded off)’ + major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger round muscle’ (vs teres minor above it).
origin: Dorsal surface of the inferior angle of scapula
insertion: Medial lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of humerus
tip: NOT part of the rotator cuff — it is “lat’s little helper”; mnemonic: “a lady between two majors” (lat dorsi inserts between pec major and teres major).

name: Biceps brachii
etymology: From Latin bi- ‘two’ + caput ‘head’ (biceps, ‘two-headed’) + brachii ‘of the arm’ (brachium). So it means ‘the two-headed muscle of the arm’.
origin: Long head: supraglenoid tubercle of scapula and superior glenoid labrum; short head: apex of the coracoid process of scapula
insertion: Radial tuberosity, and via the bicipital aponeurosis into the deep fascia of the medial forearm
tip: Biceps reflex tests C5–C6; it is a powerful supinator — think of turning a screwdriver clockwise with the right hand.

name: Biceps brachii — long head
etymology: From Latin bi- ‘two’ + caput ‘head’ (biceps, ‘two-headed’) + brachii ‘of the arm’ (brachium). So it means ‘the two-headed muscle of the arm’. The ‘long head’ has the longer tendon, running from above the glenoid through the shoulder joint.
origin: Supraglenoid tubercle of scapula and superior glenoid labrum (tendon runs intra-articularly then down the intertubercular groove)
insertion: Radial tuberosity and bicipital aponeurosis (common tendon with short head)
actions: Stabilises the humeral head (depresses it in the glenoid)
tip: Site of SLAP lesions and bicipital tendinopathy in the groove; a rupture gives the “Popeye” bulge. Incline curls stretch it.

name: Biceps brachii — short head
etymology: From Latin bi- ‘two’ + caput ‘head’ (biceps, ‘two-headed’) + brachii ‘of the arm’ (brachium). So it means ‘the two-headed muscle of the arm’. The ‘short head’ has the shorter tendon, arising from the coracoid process.
origin: Apex of the coracoid process of scapula (with coracobrachialis)
insertion: Radial tuberosity and bicipital aponeurosis (common tendon with long head)
tip: Shares the coracoid origin with coracobrachialis and pec minor’s insertion; preacher and spider curls (arm in front) bias it.

name: Brachialis
etymology: From Latin brachialis ‘of the arm’ (brachium, arm). So it simply means ‘the arm muscle’ — the deep flexor lying on the front of the humerus.
origin: Distal half of the anterior surface of the humerus
insertion: Coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna
innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6); small lateral part by the radial nerve (C7)
tip: The “workhorse” elbow flexor — it inserts on the ulna, so forearm rotation does not change its leverage; hammer and reverse curls emphasise it.

name: Coracobrachialis
etymology: From Greek korax ‘raven’ (the coracoid process looks like a raven’s beak) + Latin brachium ‘arm’. So it means ‘the muscle from the coracoid to the arm’.
origin: Apex of the coracoid process of scapula (with short head of biceps)
insertion: Middle third of the medial surface of the humerus
tip: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces it — a handy landmark in the axilla.

name: Triceps brachii
etymology: From Latin tri- ‘three’ + caput ‘head’ (triceps, ‘three-headed’) + brachii ‘of the arm’ (brachium). So it means ‘the three-headed muscle of the arm’.
origin: Long head: infraglenoid tubercle of scapula; lateral head: posterior humerus above (lateral to) the radial groove; medial head: posterior humerus below (medial to) the radial groove
insertion: Posterior surface of the olecranon process of ulna (and deep fascia of forearm)
tip: Triceps reflex tests C7; the long head crosses the shoulder, so overhead extensions stretch it most.

name: Triceps brachii — long head
etymology: From Latin tri- ‘three’ + caput ‘head’ (triceps, ‘three-headed’) + brachii ‘of the arm’ (brachium). So it means ‘the three-headed muscle of the arm’. The ‘long head’ is the longest, arising from the scapula and crossing the shoulder.
origin: Infraglenoid tubercle of scapula
insertion: Posterior surface of the olecranon process of ulna (common tendon)
tip: The only biarticular head — overhead extensions and pullovers stretch it; it forms borders of the quadrangular and triangular spaces.

name: Triceps brachii — lateral head
etymology: From Latin tri- ‘three’ + caput ‘head’ (triceps, ‘three-headed’) + brachii ‘of the arm’ (brachium). So it means ‘the three-headed muscle of the arm’. The ‘lateral head’ lies on the outer side of the back of the arm.
origin: Posterior surface of humerus, superior (lateral) to the radial groove
insertion: Posterior surface of the olecranon process of ulna (common tendon)
tip: Gives the “horseshoe” shape on the outer arm; pushdowns with a neutral grip load it well.

name: Triceps brachii — medial head
etymology: From Latin tri- ‘three’ + caput ‘head’ (triceps, ‘three-headed’) + brachii ‘of the arm’ (brachium). So it means ‘the three-headed muscle of the arm’. The ‘medial head’ lies deep and toward the inner side, below the radial groove.
origin: Posterior surface of humerus, inferior (medial) to the radial groove
insertion: Posterior surface of the olecranon process of ulna (common tendon) and elbow joint capsule
actions: Elbow extension (active in all extension, even low load)
tip: The workhorse of elbow extension; the radial nerve runs in the groove between it and the lateral head — at risk in humeral shaft fractures.

name: Pronator teres
etymology: From Latin pronator ‘one that turns face-down’ (pronus, bent forward) + teres ‘round, smooth’. So it means ‘the rounded pronator’.
origin: Humeral (superficial) head: medial epicondyle (common flexor origin) and medial supracondylar ridge; ulnar (deep) head: medial side of the coronoid process of ulna
insertion: Middle of the lateral surface of the radius (pronator tuberosity, point of maximum convexity)
tip: The median nerve passes between its two heads — compression here (pronator syndrome) mimics carpal tunnel but includes palm numbness.

name: Flexor carpi radialis
etymology: From Latin flexor ‘bender’ + carpi ‘of the wrist’ (Greek karpos) + radialis ‘of the radius (radial side)’. So it means ‘the wrist flexor on the radial side’.
origin: Medial epicondyle of humerus (common flexor tendon)
insertion: Base of the 2nd metacarpal (and slip to the 3rd)
tip: Its tendon is the landmark for the radial pulse (artery just lateral) — part of the common flexor origin stressed in medial epicondylalgia (golfer’s elbow).

name: Palmaris longus
etymology: From Latin palmaris ‘of the palm’ (palma) + longus ‘long’. So it means ‘the long muscle of the palm’ — a long tendon into the palmar aponeurosis.
origin: Medial epicondyle of humerus (common flexor tendon)
insertion: Distal half of the flexor retinaculum and the palmar aponeurosis
tip: Absent in roughly 1 in 7 people; passes superficial to the carpal tunnel and is a favourite tendon graft (e.g. UCL “Tommy John” reconstruction).

name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
parts: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris
etymology: From Latin flexor ‘bender’ + carpi ‘of the wrist’ + ulnaris ‘of the ulna (ulnar side)’. So it means ‘the wrist flexor on the ulnar side’.
origin: Humeral head: medial epicondyle (common flexor tendon); ulnar head: medial margin of olecranon and proximal two-thirds of the posterior border of ulna
insertion: Pisiform, then via pisohamate ligament to hook of hamate and pisometacarpal ligament to base of 5th metacarpal
tip: The ulnar nerve enters the forearm between its two heads (cubital tunnel) — a site of entrapment; the only anterior forearm muscle fully supplied by the ulnar nerve besides the medial FDP.

name: Flexor digitorum superficialis
parts: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis
etymology: From Latin flexor ‘bender’ + digitorum ‘of the fingers’ (digitus) + superficialis ‘on the surface’. So it means ‘the superficial finger flexor’ (above flexor digitorum profundus).
origin: Humero-ulnar head: medial epicondyle (common flexor tendon), ulnar collateral ligament and coronoid process of ulna; radial head: superior half of anterior border of radius (oblique line)
insertion: Sides of the middle phalanges of digits 2–5 (each tendon splits around the FDP tendon)
tip: Its four tendons pass through the carpal tunnel — test it by flexing one finger’s PIP while the others are held in extension.

name: Flexor digitorum profundus
etymology: From Latin flexor ‘bender’ + digitorum ‘of the fingers’ + profundus ‘deep’. So it means ‘the deep finger flexor’.
origin: Proximal three-quarters of the anterior and medial surfaces of ulna and adjacent interosseous membrane
insertion: Bases of the distal phalanges of digits 2–5 (palmar surface)
innervation: Medial part (digits 4–5): ulnar nerve (C8–T1); lateral part (digits 2–3): anterior interosseous branch of median nerve (C8–T1)
tip: The only muscle that flexes the DIP joints; its tendons run through the carpal tunnel, and avulsion from the ring finger is “jersey finger”.

name: Flexor pollicis longus
etymology: From Latin flexor ‘bender’ + pollicis ‘of the thumb’ (pollex) + longus ‘long’. So it means ‘the long flexor of the thumb’.
origin: Anterior surface of the radius and adjacent interosseous membrane (variable slip from coronoid process/medial epicondyle)
insertion: Palmar base of the distal phalanx of the thumb
innervation: Anterior interosseous branch of median nerve (C7–C8)
tip: Its tendon runs through the carpal tunnel; anterior interosseous nerve palsy weakens FPL and index FDP so the patient cannot make a round “OK” sign.

name: Pronator quadratus
etymology: From Latin pronator ‘one that turns face-down’ + quadratus ‘squared, four-sided’. So it means ‘the square pronator’ across the distal forearm.
origin: Distal quarter of the anterior surface of the ulna
insertion: Distal quarter of the anterior surface of the radius
actions: Holds radius and ulna together at the distal radioulnar joint
innervation: Anterior interosseous branch of median nerve (C7–C8)
tip: The main pronator in all elbow positions — pronator teres joins in for fast or resisted pronation.

name: Brachioradialis
etymology: From Latin brachium ‘arm’ + radialis ‘of the radius’. So it means ‘the muscle from the arm (humerus) to the radius’.
origin: Proximal two-thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge of humerus
insertion: Lateral surface of the distal radius, just proximal to the radial styloid process
actions: Elbow flexion (strongest with forearm in mid-prone/neutral)
Returns forearm to mid-prone from full pronation or supination
tip: An elbow flexor supplied by the radial (“extensor”) nerve; hammer curls target it and its reflex tests C6.

name: Extensor carpi radialis longus
etymology: From Latin extensor ‘stretcher, straightener’ + carpi ‘of the wrist’ + radialis ‘radial side’ + longus ‘long’. So it means ‘the long radial wrist extensor’.
origin: Distal third of the lateral supracondylar ridge of humerus
insertion: Dorsal surface of the base of the 2nd metacarpal
tip: Works with ECRB to hold the wrist extended during gripping, giving the finger flexors optimal length.

name: Extensor carpi radialis brevis
etymology: From Latin extensor ‘straightener’ + carpi ‘of the wrist’ + radialis ‘radial side’ + brevis ‘short’. So it means ‘the short radial wrist extensor’.
origin: Lateral epicondyle of humerus (common extensor tendon)
insertion: Dorsal surface of the base of the 3rd metacarpal
tip: Its origin is the usual site of lateral epicondylalgia (tennis elbow) — progressive eccentric wrist-extension loading is first-line rehab.

name: Extensor digitorum
etymology: From Latin extensor ‘straightener’ + digitorum ‘of the fingers’. So it means ‘the extensor of the fingers’.
origin: Lateral epicondyle of humerus (common extensor tendon)
insertion: Extensor (dorsal digital) expansions of digits 2–5, to bases of middle and distal phalanges
actions: Finger IP extension (with lumbricals and interossei)
innervation: Posterior interosseous nerve, deep branch of radial (C7–C8)
tip: Linked by intertendinous connections on the back of the hand — the reason it is hard to lift your ring finger alone.

name: Extensor digiti minimi
etymology: From Latin extensor ‘straightener’ + digiti minimi ‘of the smallest finger’. So it means ‘the extensor of the little finger’.
origin: Lateral epicondyle of humerus (common extensor tendon)
insertion: Extensor expansion of the 5th digit
actions: Little finger MCP and IP extension
innervation: Posterior interosseous nerve, deep branch of radial (C7–C8)
tip: Lets you extend the little finger independently — the “pinky out” muscle.

name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
parts: Humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris
etymology: From Latin extensor ‘straightener’ + carpi ‘of the wrist’ + ulnaris ‘of the ulna (ulnar side)’. So it means ‘the wrist extensor on the ulnar side’.
origin: Humeral head: lateral epicondyle (common extensor tendon); ulnar head: posterior border of ulna (by aponeurosis)
insertion: Medial (dorsal) side of the base of the 5th metacarpal
innervation: Posterior interosseous nerve, deep branch of radial (C7–C8)
tip: Its tendon can sublux over the ulnar head — a cause of ulnar-sided wrist pain in racquet and golf athletes.

name: Anconeus
etymology: From Greek ankōn ‘elbow’ (via Latin anconeus). So it means ‘the elbow muscle’.
origin: Posterior surface of the lateral epicondyle of humerus
insertion: Lateral surface of the olecranon and superior part of the posterior surface of ulna
tip: A small triangular extension of the triceps; it tensions the posterolateral capsule and helps stabilise the elbow.

name: Supinator
etymology: From Latin supinare ‘to lay on the back, turn palm-up’ (supinus, lying face up). So it means ‘the muscle that turns the palm up’.
origin: Lateral epicondyle of humerus, radial collateral and annular ligaments, supinator crest and fossa of ulna
insertion: Lateral, posterior and anterior surfaces of the proximal third of the radius
actions: Forearm supination (especially with elbow extended or slow, unresisted)
tip: The posterior interosseous nerve passes through it (arcade of Frohse) — radial tunnel syndrome mimics tennis elbow.

name: Abductor pollicis longus
etymology: From Latin abductor ‘one that leads away’ (ab ‘away’ + ducere ‘to lead’) + pollicis ‘of the thumb’ + longus ‘long’. So it means ‘the long muscle that leads the thumb away’.
origin: Posterior surfaces of the proximal halves of ulna and radius and the interosseous membrane
insertion: Lateral side of the base of the 1st metacarpal
actions: Thumb abduction at the CMC joint
Thumb extension at the CMC joint
innervation: Posterior interosseous nerve, deep branch of radial (C7–C8)
tip: With EPB it forms the first dorsal compartment — inflamed in De Quervain’s tenosynovitis (Finkelstein test); the pair bounds the anatomical snuffbox radially.

name: Extensor pollicis brevis
etymology: From Latin extensor ‘straightener’ + pollicis ‘of the thumb’ + brevis ‘short’. So it means ‘the short extensor of the thumb’.
origin: Posterior surface of the distal third of the radius and the interosseous membrane
insertion: Dorsal base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb
innervation: Posterior interosseous nerve, deep branch of radial (C7–C8)
tip: Shares the first dorsal compartment with APL (De Quervain’s); forms the radial border of the anatomical snuffbox.

name: Extensor pollicis longus
etymology: From Latin extensor ‘straightener’ + pollicis ‘of the thumb’ + longus ‘long’. So it means ‘the long extensor of the thumb’.
origin: Posterior surface of the middle third of the ulna and the interosseous membrane
insertion: Dorsal base of the distal phalanx of the thumb
actions: Thumb retroposition (lifts thumb off the table)
innervation: Posterior interosseous nerve, deep branch of radial (C7–C8)
tip: Hooks around Lister’s tubercle and forms the ulnar border of the anatomical snuffbox; can rupture weeks after a distal radius fracture.

name: Extensor indicis
etymology: From Latin extensor ‘straightener’ + indicis ‘of the pointer (index finger)’ (index, ‘one that points out’). So it means ‘the extensor of the pointing finger’.
origin: Posterior surface of the distal third of the ulna and the interosseous membrane
insertion: Extensor expansion of the index finger (ulnar side of the extensor digitorum tendon)
actions: Index finger MCP and IP extension (independent pointing)
innervation: Posterior interosseous nerve, deep branch of radial (C7–C8)
tip: Gives the index finger independent extension — the “pointing” muscle; its tendon is sometimes transferred to replace a ruptured EPL.

name: Abductor pollicis brevis
etymology: From Latin abductor ‘one that leads away’ + pollicis ‘of the thumb’ + brevis ‘short’. So it means ‘the short muscle that leads the thumb away’.
origin: Flexor retinaculum and the tubercles of the scaphoid and trapezium
insertion: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb
tip: The most superficial thenar muscle — weakness and wasting here is a classic sign of advanced carpal tunnel syndrome.

name: Flexor pollicis brevis
parts: Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis
Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis
etymology: From Latin flexor ‘bender’ + pollicis ‘of the thumb’ + brevis ‘short’. So it means ‘the short flexor of the thumb’.
origin: Superficial head: flexor retinaculum and tubercle of trapezium; deep head: trapezoid and capitate
insertion: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb (via the radial sesamoid)
innervation: Superficial head: recurrent branch of median nerve (C8–T1); deep head: deep branch of ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
tip: Dual nerve supply means thumb flexion is often partly spared in an isolated median or ulnar nerve lesion.

name: Opponens pollicis
etymology: From Latin opponens ‘placing against’ (ob ‘against’ + ponere ‘to place’) + pollicis ‘of the thumb’. So it means ‘the muscle that sets the thumb against the fingers’.
origin: Flexor retinaculum and tubercle of trapezium
insertion: Entire lateral border of the 1st metacarpal
actions: Thumb opposition (flexes and medially rotates the 1st metacarpal at the CMC joint)
tip: Opposition is what makes the human grip — loss of it (median nerve injury) gives the flat “ape hand”.

name: Adductor pollicis
etymology: From Latin adductor ‘one that leads toward’ (ad ‘toward’ + ducere ‘to lead’) + pollicis ‘of the thumb’. So it means ‘the muscle that draws the thumb toward the palm’.
origin: Oblique head: bases of 2nd and 3rd metacarpals, capitate and adjacent carpals; transverse head: anterior surface of the shaft of the 3rd metacarpal
insertion: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb (via the ulnar sesamoid)
tip: Ulnar nerve palsy weakens it — Froment’s sign: the patient flexes the thumb IP (using FPL) to hold paper in a key pinch.

name: Abductor digiti minimi (hand)
etymology: From Latin abductor ‘one that leads away’ + digiti minimi ‘of the smallest finger’. So it means ‘the muscle that leads the little finger away’.
origin: Pisiform and tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris (pisohamate ligament)
insertion: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the 5th digit
tip: The most superficial and medial hypothenar muscle — its wasting is an early sign of ulnar neuropathy.

name: Flexor digiti minimi brevis (hand)
etymology: From Latin flexor ‘bender’ + digiti minimi ‘of the smallest finger’ + brevis ‘short’. So it means ‘the short flexor of the little finger’.
origin: Hook of hamate and flexor retinaculum
insertion: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the 5th digit
tip: Part of the hypothenar eminence with ADM and opponens digiti minimi; often fused with ADM.

name: Opponens digiti minimi (hand)
parts: Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand
etymology: From Latin opponens ‘placing against’ + digiti minimi ‘of the smallest finger’. So it means ‘the muscle that sets the little finger against the thumb’.
origin: Hook of hamate and flexor retinaculum
insertion: Medial border of the 5th metacarpal
actions: Opposition of the little finger (draws the 5th metacarpal anteriorly and rotates it laterally)
Deepens the hollow of the palm (cupping)
tip: Helps cup the palm for gripping round objects, working with opponens pollicis.

name: Lumbricals of the hand
etymology: From Latin lumbricus ‘earthworm’. So it means ‘the earthworm-like muscles’ — four slender worm-shaped strands in the palm.
origin: Tendons of flexor digitorum profundus (1st and 2nd: radial sides of tendons to digits 2–3; 3rd and 4th: adjacent sides of tendons to digits 3–5)
insertion: Lateral (radial) sides of the extensor expansions of digits 2–5
innervation: Lumbricals 1–2: median nerve (C8–T1); lumbricals 3–4: deep branch of ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
tip: They create the “table-top” position (MCP flexed, IPs straight); unusually, they arise from a tendon rather than bone.

name: Dorsal interossei of the hand
etymology: From Latin dorsalis ‘of the back’ + inter ‘between’ + os/ossis ‘bone’. So it means ‘the muscles between the bones on the back of the hand’ (between the metacarpals).
origin: Adjacent sides of the 1st–5th metacarpals (four bipennate muscles)
insertion: Bases of the proximal phalanges and extensor expansions of digits 2–4 (radial side of 2nd and 3rd; ulnar side of 3rd and 4th)
actions: Finger abduction (digits 2–4, away from the axis of the middle finger)
tip: Mnemonic DAB — Dorsal ABduct; the 1st dorsal interosseous is the bulge between thumb and index and wastes visibly in ulnar palsy.

name: Palmar interossei
etymology: From Latin palmaris ‘of the palm’ + inter ‘between’ + os/ossis ‘bone’. So it means ‘the muscles between the bones on the palm side’ (between the metacarpals).
origin: Palmar surfaces of the 2nd, 4th and 5th metacarpals (unipennate; ulnar side of 2nd, radial sides of 4th and 5th)
insertion: Bases of the proximal phalanges and extensor expansions of digits 2, 4 and 5
actions: Finger adduction (digits 2, 4, 5 toward the middle finger)
tip: Mnemonic PAD — Palmar ADduct; test by gripping a card between straight fingers (card test for ulnar nerve).
